## Summary

- Problem: Plugins can expose gateway-authenticated HTTP routes, but there was no generic way for a plugin to register a first-class Control UI navigation entry.
- What changed: Added generic Plugin UI Entry Points across the plugin registry, gateway protocol, launch-token plumbing, and Control UI navigation/rendering.
- Security follow-up: Plugin UI entry registration, launch/session auth, and iframe bridge proxying now validate canonical decoded plugin roots, so encoded dot-segment paths cannot let one plugin UI session authorize sibling plugin routes.
- Scope boundary: This PR does not add the Session Search plugin or any plugin-specific UI. The proof plugin lives separately on [`Ittiz/openclaw@forge/session-search-plugin`](https://github.com/Ittiz/openclaw/tree/forge/session-search-plugin).

## What Problem This Solves

Plugins can expose gateway-authenticated HTTP routes, but before this PR they had no generic, first-class way to place a Control UI navigation entry that launches a plugin-owned UI through the gateway authorization boundary. This PR adds that contract while keeping plugin entry paths and iframe bridge requests confined to the owning plugin root.

## Working Example Plugin

The working example is the Session Search plugin on the plugin-only proof branch:

- Branch: [`Ittiz/openclaw@forge/session-search-plugin`](https://github.com/Ittiz/openclaw/tree/forge/session-search-plugin)

target.title: Fix/OpenAI device code request timeout
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where operators running OpenAI Codex device-code login (`openclaw models auth login --provider openai --device-code`, or the equivalent configure/wizard auth choice) could hang forever when a single `auth.openai.com` HTTP request stopped responding.

Before this patch, the flow enforced a 15-minute poll-loop deadline around authorization waiting, and callers could cancel via `AbortSignal`, but the three HTTP calls for user-code request, authorization poll, and token exchange had no per-request operation deadline covering both headers and body reads. A stalled TCP/proxy/blackhole response, or a server that returned headers and then stalled the body, could leave the CLI spinner stuck.

## Why This Change Was Made

Treat each device-code HTTP call as one timed operation: headers fetch plus bounded body read under `buildOAuthRequestSignal` (caller `AbortSignal` composed with `AbortSignal.timeout`, 30s, aligned with the sibling ChatGPT browser OAuth token request timeout). Poll requests clamp that timeout to the remaining 15-minute authorization deadline and retry only on operation timeout (including post-header body stalls) until the overall deadline expires. Caller cancel (Ctrl-C / wizard abort) remains distinguishable and does not retry. User-code and token-exchange timeouts fail fast with a clear error.

Body/fetch aborts rethrow the composed signal reason so undici `AbortError` collapse does not erase `TimeoutError` vs caller cancel distinguishability.

Scope stays OpenAI Codex device-code login HTTP only; browser OAuth and other providers are unchanged.

## User Impact

**Before:** A hung device-code HTTP request (or a post-header body stall) could block `models auth login --device-code` indefinitely, even past the advertised 15-minute authorization window, while still depending on the overall poll deadline for happy-path waiting.

**After:** Each device-code request+body read aborts after 30 seconds (or sooner near the overall deadline). Poll timeouts retry within the 15-minute window; caller cancel aborts immediately without retry; user-code and token-exchange stalls surface an explicit timeout error instead of hanging forever.

## Evidence

- `extensions/openai/openai-chatgpt-device-code.ts` — `buildOAuthRequestSignal` composes caller cancel + 30s operation deadline across fetch + body read; poll retries only on operation timeout
- Regression: `extensions/openai/openai-chatgpt-device-code.test.ts`
  - hung user-code / token-exchange abort with timeout error
  - poll retries after `TimeoutError` and completes
  - caller cancel during hung fetch / poll wait / post-header body stall does not retry or map to timeout
  - real `node:http` partial-body stall coverage
  - success path asserts fetches carry an `AbortSignal`

### Unit regression

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed:** OpenAI Codex device-code login no longer leaves individual HTTP operations unbounded when the remote endpoint stops responding before headers return, or returns headers and then stalls the body; caller cancel remains distinct from operation timeout.
- **Canonical reachability path:** Operator runs device-code auth → `loginOpenAICodexDeviceCode` → `requestOpenAICodexDeviceCode` / `pollOpenAICodexDeviceCode` / `exchangeOpenAICodexDeviceCode` → `runOpenAICodexDeviceCodeRequest` → `buildOAuthRequestSignal` (`AbortSignal.any([caller, AbortSignal.timeout(...)])`) + `readOpenAICodexDeviceBody`.

Only `AbortSignal.timeout` duration is shortened for deterministic hang repro; production fetch+body composition, caller composition, and error/retry mapping stay unmocked.
- **Shared helper / provider constraint check:** Reuses `buildOAuthRequestSignal` from `openai-chatgpt-oauth-abort.runtime` (same helper as ChatGPT OAuth). 30s matches the existing OpenAI ChatGPT OAuth token request timeout. Preserves current-main caller `AbortSignal` cancellation from provider sign-in. Does not migrate this path onto `fetchWithSsrFGuard` in this change.

target.title: fix(line): cap user profile cache
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an unbounded in-process `userProfileCache` in the LINE send path (`extensions/line/src/send.ts`). Profile lookups are cached for 5 minutes (TTL) but had no entry-count cap, so gateways serving many distinct LINE users accumulate Map entries indefinitely until process restart.

**Concrete scenario:** A LINE gateway processing inbound messages from 10 000 distinct users over several hours caches each `getUserProfile` result. With no size cap, the cache grows without bound.

## Why This Change Was Made

Adds a 1 024-entry cap via the existing `pruneMapToMaxSize` helper from `openclaw/plugin-sdk/collection-runtime`, matching Slack / Discord / Nextcloud Talk channel caches.

`touchLineUserProfileCache` deletes + sets so Map insertion order refreshes on both write and TTL-valid read hits (same LRU-on-access pattern as `extensions/slack/src/channel-type.ts`). Active users stay under the cap; idle oldest-inserted entries evict first.

No config/env knobs. TTL behavior is unchanged.

## User Impact

**Before:** Long-lived LINE gateways accumulate one `userProfileCache` entry per distinct user indefinitely.

**After:** Cache stays at ≤ 1 024 entries. Recently touched profiles survive eviction; untouched oldest entries are pruned. First 1 024 distinct users behave as before until the cap is exceeded.

## Evidence

- `extensions/line/src/send.ts` — `LINE_USER_PROFILE_CACHE_MAX_ENTRIES = 1024`, `touchLineUserProfileCache` (delete + set + `pruneMapToMaxSize`) on write and TTL hit
- `extensions/line/src/monitor.ts` — inbound path calls `getUserDisplayName` → `getUserProfile`

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users running OC Path against JSONC input above the 16 MiB byte cap could receive normal empty or not-found output instead of a typed size rejection. Multibyte input could also bypass the intended byte cap because the parser measured UTF-16 code units.

## Why This Change Was Made

The shared JSONC parser now measures UTF-8 bytes before the empty-input shortcut and `parseTree`. The OC Path CLI loader propagates the existing `OC_JSONC_INPUT_TOO_LARGE` diagnostic through its structured error path for every verb that loads JSON/JSONC, without changing other parser-warning behavior or adding another limit.

## User Impact

OC Path now consistently rejects oversized multibyte and whitespace-only JSONC before allocating the parse tree, and CLI callers receive the documented machine-readable diagnostic instead of a misleading normal result.

## Evidence

- Current head: `ce5851cf0cee7636dd5f30ed45994fdd7c77c9f0`.
- Real CLI behavior: the production `registerPathCli` Commander registration was bundled from this head and invoked as `openclaw path resolve oc://oversized.json/value --cwd <fixture> --json` against a 16,777,220-byte UTF-8 JSON fixture. The command produced:

target.title: fix(reef): bound inbox websocket open waits at 30s
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Reef inbox monitoring uses the WHATWG `WebSocket` (not the `ws` package), so there is no `handshakeTimeout` option. `ReefInboxConnection.live()` only settles on `close` / `error` / channel `abort`. When a peer accepts TCP but never completes the websocket upgrade, `start()` waits forever on `await live()` and the reconnect backoff loop never advances.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Add a private `REEF_INBOX_WEBSOCKET_OPEN_TIMEOUT_MS = 30_000` open-wait floor inside `live()`.
- On timeout: reject with `reef inbox websocket open timed out` (before `close`) so `start()` takes the existing catch/backoff path.
- Clear the timer on successful `open` so healthy long-lived inbox sockets are unaffected.
- Optional constructor `openTimeoutMs` defaults to 30s for production; tests use a short stand-in.

No new config/env surface. Does not switch Reef onto the `ws` package.

Note: open [#106456](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/106456) bounds relay HTTP JSON reads in the same `transport.ts`; this PR only touches the inbox websocket open wait and should rebase cleanly.

## User Impact

**Before:** A Reef relay that accepted TCP without completing the websocket handshake could pin the inbox reconnect loop forever until the channel aborted.

**After:** Open waits fail closed after 30s and the existing reconnect backoff continues.

## Evidence

- Changed: `extensions/reef/src/transport.ts`
- Production caller: `extensions/reef/src/channel.ts` → `ReefInboxConnection.start`
- Sibling intent: Slack/Mattermost/Signal 30s handshake floors (Reef cannot use `ws` `handshakeTimeout`)
- Regression: `extensions/reef/src/transport.test.ts`

### Caller-path Vitest

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/reef/src/transport.test.ts --reporter=verbose
```

```text
 ✓ uses a 30s open-wait floor because WHATWG WebSocket has no handshakeTimeout
[reef open-wait proof] timeout_then_reconnect=true socket_attempts=2 openTimeout_ms=40
 ✓ returns control to reconnect when the websocket never opens 309ms
[reef open-wait live proof] timed_out=true elapsed_ms=506 openTimeout_ms=200
 ✓ fails open against a TCP peer that never completes the websocket upgrade 532ms
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  6 passed (6)
```

## Real behavior proof

**Commands run:**
```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/reef/src/transport.test.ts --reporter=verbose
```

**Before fix:**
`live()` had no open-wait timer; a never-opening socket left `start()` blocked until channel abort.

**After fix:**
Production default open-wait is 30s. Against a hang factory / TCP peer that never upgrades, `live()` rejects and `start()` reconnects.

**Evidence after fix:**
```text
[reef open-wait proof] timeout_then_reconnect=true socket_attempts=2 openTimeout_ms=40
[reef open-wait live proof] timed_out=true elapsed_ms=506 openTimeout_ms=200
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  6 passed (6)
```

**What was not tested:**
Live Reef relay credentials; full 30s production floor (tests use 40ms / 200ms stand-ins with source wiring asserting `30_000`); REST `fetch` hang floors on `ReefTransportClient.request` (separate surface; see also #106456).

target.title: feat: add readiness conditions and providers
target.body:
Related RFC: https://github.com/openclaw/rfcs/pull/33

## Problem

OpenClaw already exposes Gateway `/ready` and `/readyz`, but readiness is evaluated by a fixed set of Gateway checks. Hosts and operators cannot select the additional criteria that define readiness for a deployment, plugins cannot contribute bounded observational evidence, and CLI, health, and status surfaces do not share one canonical result.

That leaves Docker, Kubernetes, systemd, OCC, and other hosts maintaining private scripts to answer a basic question: is this OpenClaw instance ready to accept work under its configured requirements?

## Proposal

This draft implements the readiness portion of RFC 0018:

- normalize Gateway startup, admission, drain, selected-channel, suppressed-channel, event-loop, and workspace evidence into structured conditions
- distinguish required conditions, which fail readiness on `False` or `Unknown`, from advisory conditions, which remain visible without changing the ready result
- let operators select built-in and plugin-contributed criteria directly with `gateway.readiness`
- let activated plugins register namespaced, self-describing criteria through the public plugin registry
- bound plugin checks with per-criterion timeouts, an overall readiness deadline, stable timeout/error results, short caching, and in-flight coalescing
- project the same canonical result through `/ready`, `/readyz`, Gateway `ready`, health, status, and `openclaw ready`
- provide human-readable and `--json` CLI output with fail-closed exit status

Example operator selection:

```json5
{
  gateway: {
    readiness: {
      requiredCriteria: ["openclaw.workspace-writable", "plugin.example.dependency"],
      advisoryCriteria: ["plugin.metrics.exporter"],
    },
  },
}
```

A plugin may contribute observational evidence without changing readiness by default:

```ts
api.registerReadinessCriterion({
  id: "dependency",
  description: "Example dependency is reachable",
  async check({ pluginConfig, signal }) {
    const reachable = await probeDependency(pluginConfig, { signal });
    return reachable
      ? { status: "True", reason: "DependencyReachable" }
      : { status: "False", reason: "DependencyUnavailable" };
  },
});
```

Core publishes that registration as `plugin.<plugin-id>.dependency`. Operators explicitly select it as `requiredCriteria` when it belongs in their serving contract.

## Compatibility

Existing `/ready` and `/readyz` routes remain available and retain their HTTP contract: `200` when all required conditions are true and `503` otherwise. Existing installations need no readiness configuration; the Gateway lifecycle baseline always applies, while explicitly selected criteria add richer deployment-specific evidence.

This PR does **not** add hosting profiles, profile selection, node-mode profiles, runtime activation identity, release conformance, Lobster concepts, tenant concepts, OCC resources, or policy/doctor dependencies. Standard Hosting Profiles are intentionally separated into RFC 0023 so this readiness facility can stand on its own.

## Review Stack

This is one upstream PR with four commits. The fork PRs preserve the same smaller review boundaries:

- [PR 17: canonical Gateway readiness conditions](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/17)
- [PR 22: workspace writability criterion](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/22)
- [PR 23: selectable readiness providers](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/23)
- [PR 27: canonical `openclaw ready` CLI](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/27)

The branch is rebased onto current `openclaw/main`; the plugin registration slice is adapted to the current modular registry.

## Validation

- exact head: `d82da685c500b71292feddb992e7addc698a7328`
- 12 focused readiness, plugin registry, configuration, Gateway HTTP/RPC, status, and CLI files pass: 96 assertions across 7 Vitest shards
- formatting and `git diff --check` pass
- package build and tarball-integrity checks pass; the plugin SDK declaration graph remains within budget and required exports are present
- Codex review findings fixed: the CLI calls the canonical Gateway evaluator, live readiness is projected through health and status RPCs, and text status avoids a readiness RPC it does not render
- ClawSweeper findings fixed: workspace probing is observational and canonical config help/label metadata covers `gateway.readiness`
- packaged Docker proof passes from the exact checkout: package version `2026.7.2`, image `sha256:6448ba902d74aacfc25a4456572ec0c42448dca7507aa5a64ab348ef12347518`
- the package-installed Gateway proves `/ready` and `/readyz` return `200`, a required missing workspace changes readiness to `503` while `/healthz` remains `200`, restoring the workspace returns readiness to `200`, and `openclaw ready --json` exits `0 -> 1 -> 0` with the same structured condition
- the packaged proof found and drove a fix for a missing lazy Gateway `ready` RPC binding; the existing descriptor-to-dispatch regression guard now covers the live path and preserves append-only method ordering

Full local typecheck is not claimed: the shared dependency tree has unrelated baseline errors, and this machine runs Node 24.14 while current OpenClaw requires Node 24.15+ for the embedded SQLite safety floor.

target.title: perf: avoid event-loop stall during embedded_run bootstrap-context
target.body:
## Summary

Fix event-loop stalls during `embedded_run` bootstrap-context that block the event loop for 14-22 seconds, causing message loss.

## What Problem This Solves

Event-loop stalls during `embedded_run` bootstrap-context loading, caused by synchronous I/O and a blocking `fs.glob` walk over large workspaces, block the loop for 14-22 seconds and drop messages (issue #87509 reports 14-22s bootstrap-context stalls that block channel I/O, WebSocket keepalive, and timers).

### Root causes addressed

1. **Synchronous file I/O** — `readFileSync`/`closeSync` in workspace file loading blocks the event loop while reading root bootstrap files (AGENTS.md, SOUL.md, etc.)
2. **Unbounded blocking glob walks** — `fs.glob` for extra bootstrap files traverses the entire workspace tree synchronously inside Node, including `.git`/`node_modules` directories, without yielding to the event loop
3. **Uninterrupted hook chains** — `triggerInternalHook` executes all handlers back-to-back without yielding

## Why This Change Was Made

Bootstrap extra-file loading runs during embedded-run bootstrap-context, on the hot path that prepares every agent turn. On `main` the exported loader reaches Node `fs.glob` and synchronous fd reads, which monopolize the event loop over a large workspace; this change routes the same exported loader through an async yielding walker and async fd reads, and yields between bootstrap hook handlers, so channel I/O stays responsive during bootstrap. The public plugin SDK surface is deliberately unchanged.

### Changes

**`src/agents/workspace.ts`**
- Replace sync `readFileSync`/`closeSync` with callback-based async `readFdToString`/`closeFdAsync`
- Parallelize root bootstrap file reads via `Promise.all` (previously serial `for` loop)
- Replace `fs.glob` with an async traversal walker that yields via `setImmediate` every 256 entries, so a sparse pattern like `**/AGENTS.md` over a large workspace never blocks the event loop. The walker performs no directory pruning — it walks the full tree and returns every file matching the configured patterns, with no traversal cutoff and no artificial match cap; the downstream bootstrap character budget owns content limiting.
- Preserve `fs.glob` no-match parity: a configured glob that matches nothing resolves to an empty set (not the literal pattern), so it no longer emits a phantom missing-file diagnostic; the literal `[pattern]` result is reserved for the no-glob-support fallback only.
- Preserve `fs.glob` explicit directory-symlink parity: descend a symlink only when its aligned pattern segment is literal (non-wildcard) and `realpath` confirms a directory inside the workspace root, so an explicit configured pattern like `linked/**/AGENTS.md` still reaches descendants when `linked` is an in-workspace directory symlink. Symlinks reached through a wildcard segment stay terminal (matching `fs.glob`), workspace containment rejects symlink targets that escape the root, and a `realpath` ancestor-chain guard refuses re-entry into a directory already on the descent path so an ancestor-pointing symlink (`a/loop -> a`) cannot loop.
- Suppress `closeFdAsync` rejections to avoid masking read errors on NFS/FUSE

**`src/hooks/internal-hooks.ts`** / **`src/hooks/internal-hook-dispatch.ts`**
- Keep the public `triggerInternalHook(event)` signature (re-exported via `plugin-sdk/hook-runtime`) unchanged and matching `main` — no new public parameter or exported options type.
- Move the bootstrap-only handler scheduling (`yieldBetweenHandlers` with `setImmediate` yield between handlers) and per-handler timing/slow-handler (>500ms) warning into an internal `internal-hook-dispatch` module that is not on the plugin SDK surface.

**`src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/attempt.ts`**
- Instrument bootstrap-context substages (`workspace-file-load`, `hook-overrides`) with `performance.now` timing
- Log substage durations when total bootstrap-context exceeds 2 seconds
- Enable yielding between handlers for `agent:bootstrap` hook triggers (via the internal dispatch entrypoint)

**`src/agents/bootstrap-files.ts`** / **`src/agents/bootstrap-hooks.ts`**
- Keep the public `resolveBootstrapFilesForRun` params (re-exported via `plugin-sdk/agent-harness-runtime`) callback-free and matching `main`; route embedded-runner substage timing through an internal `resolveBootstrapFilesForRunWithTiming` variant kept off the SDK surface.
- Support the new async workspace file loading interface.

### Tests

- `workspace.test.ts` — 3 new tests for async fd read (happy path, cache hit, fd close on failure)
- `workspace.load-extra-bootstrap-files.test.ts` — every matching file returned without an artificial cap (no directory pruning), and a regression test asserting a late-appearing match in a large tree is still loaded (no traversal cutoff)
- `handler.test.ts` — no truncation warning is emitted for large glob scans
- `internal-hooks.test.ts` — yield-between-handlers ordering, handler timing reporting, and slow handler warning exercised through the internal dispatch entrypoint
- `workspace.load-extra-bootstrap-files.test.ts` — a no-match glob resolves to an empty set with no missing-file diagnostic (fs.glob parity)
- `workspace.load-extra-bootstrap-files.test.ts` — explicit directory-symlink glob parity across three states (real `fs.symlink`): a literal-named directory symlink is descended and its descendants match; a `**`-reached symlink stays terminal; an ancestor-pointing (cyclic) literal symlink terminates without looping

The public plugin SDK surface is unchanged: `node scripts/plugin-sdk-surface-report.mjs` exits 0 with no new package-exported entrypoints. All existing tests pass without modification.

## User Impact

Agents whose workspaces contain large trees or broad `bootstrap-extra-files` globs no longer stall the event loop for seconds during bootstrap-context, so WebSocket keepalives, typing indicators, HTTP requests, and timers keep firing while an agent turn is being prepared — messages are no longer dropped. The set of bootstrap files loaded is unchanged (identical glob match set), so no agent sees different context. Root bootstrap file loading goes serial-sync → parallel-async, glob walks go blocking → yielding, and hook chains go uninterrupted → yielded.

## Evidence

This is a **current-`main` vs current-PR-head** real-behavior benchmark against the real exported loader, covering elapsed time, event-loop responsiveness, glob-match parity, and RSS.

- **Behavior or issue addressed**: Event-loop stalls during `embedded_run` bootstrap-context loading caused by a blocking `fs.glob` walk over large workspaces (issue #87509). This change replaces the native `fs.glob` walk with an async walker that yields via `setImmediate` every 256 entries so the event loop stays responsive, while returning the identical configured `bootstrap-extra-files` match set.
- **Real environment tested**: OpenClaw checkout on macOS arm64, Node.js `v24.10.0`, run via `tsx` against the real exported `loadExtraBootstrapFilesWithDiagnostics` from `src/agents/workspace.ts`. `main` = `9b823c610816` (native `fs.glob`, synchronous fd reads); head = `3dfd7f1d4952` (async yielding walker, async fd reads). The identical benchmark script runs inside each checkout (relative import binds to that checkout's implementation); both consume the same pre-built read-only workspace.
- **Real environment scenario**: A workspace of **395,807 filesystem entries** (391,124 files, 4,683 dirs — wide flat dirs + a deep 40-level tree + `node_modules` + `.git` + `.hidden` noise), with `AGENTS.md` planted at several depths (root, deep-past-old-cutoff, `.hidden/`, `node_modules/`). Configured pattern `**/AGENTS.md`. During the load a 5ms repeating timer counts liveness ticks, `perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay({resolution:5})` records event-loop delay, and `process.memoryUsage().rss` is captured before/after with `global.gc()`. 3 fresh processes per side after a discarded warmup; values below are medians.
- **Failing proof before fix** (current `main` `9b823c610816`, native `fs.glob`):
  ```
  elapsed: 834.5ms
  maxEventLoopDelay: 55.5ms   meanEventLoopDelay: 8.50ms   p99: 54.9ms
  liveness timer ticks during load: 95 / 166 expected (57.2% kept)
  rssDelta: 358.3 MB
  matched bootstrap files returned: 3
  RESULT: fs.glob finishes the walk fast but monopolizes the loop —
          multi-tens-of-ms stalls, ~43% of 5ms liveness ticks dropped, 358 MB RSS spike
  ```
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch** (identical script both sides; full reproduce recipe below):
  ```
  # build the shared 395,807-entry workspace once, then run each side from its own checkout
  node --import tsx/esm --expose-gc ./bench-bootstrap.mts run "$BENCH/ws"
  ```
- **Evidence after fix** (current PR head `3dfd7f1d4952`, async yielding walker):
  ```
  elapsed: 1244.8ms
  maxEventLoopDelay: 10.7ms   meanEventLoopDelay: 5.09ms   p99: 6.6ms
  liveness timer ticks during load: 245 / 248 expected (98.8% kept)
  rssDelta: 57.0 MB
  matched bootstrap files returned: 3
  RESULT: yielding walker keeps the loop responsive — max delay near the 5ms floor,
          98.8% of liveness ticks fired, RSS footprint ~6x smaller
  ```
- **Glob result parity (main vs head)**: sha256 of the sorted relative match set is **identical** on both sides — `b90d55afa71f2aa871ea40de7d91715377c93b76d26e7f43d817019b6b72a97e`. Matched set both sides: `AGENTS.md`, the deep 40-level `deep/.../AGENTS.md`, and `node_modules/pkg000/AGENTS.md`; `.git` and `.hidden/AGENTS.md` correctly excluded by both. The custom walker changes event-loop behavior and memory, not the returned file set.

  | metric (median of 3, 395,807 entries, Node v24.10.0) | main `9b823c610816` | head `3dfd7f1d4952` |
  |---|---:|---:|
  | elapsed (ms) | 834.5 | 1244.8 |
  | max event-loop delay (ms) | 55.5 | 10.7 |
  | mean event-loop delay (ms) | 8.50 | 5.09 |
  | liveness ticks kept | 57.2% | 98.8% |
  | RSS delta (MB) | 358.3 | 57.0 |
  | `**/AGENTS.md` matches returned | 3 | 3 (identical set) |

- **Observed result after fix**: the fix trades a modest wall-clock increase (834ms → 1245ms) for the property the issue actually needs — the event loop stops stalling. Max event-loop delay drops from 55.5ms to 10.7ms (near the 5ms probe floor), liveness-tick retention rises from 57.2% to 98.8%, and peak RSS is ~6x smaller (358MB → 57MB) because the walker no longer buffers the whole `fs.glob` result eagerly. The returned match set is byte-identical (same sha256), so existing `bootstrap-extra-files` configs load the same files. At the field-report scale (much larger real workspaces), `main`'s blocking walk is what produces the 14-22s embedded_run stalls; this benchmark demonstrates the direction and mechanism (blocking `fs.glob` vs cooperative yielding) at 395,807 entries on a single dev box.
- **Reproduce**:
  ```bash
  BENCH=/tmp/bench-89040
  PR=<pr-head-checkout>
  git -C "$PR" worktree add --detach "$BENCH/main-wt" 9b823c610816   # current upstream/main
  ln -s "$PR/node_modules" "$BENCH/main-wt/node_modules"             # read-only bench, first-party deps
  cp "$BENCH/bench-bootstrap.mts" "$PR/bench-bootstrap.mts"
  cp "$BENCH/bench-bootstrap.mts" "$BENCH/main-wt/bench-bootstrap.mts"
  # build the shared workspace once (reused by both sides, walk mutates nothing)
  (cd "$PR" && node --import tsx/esm "$BENCH/bench-bootstrap.mts" build "$BENCH/ws" 400000)
  # 3 fresh processes per side, run from inside each checkout so the relative import binds
  (cd "$PR"            && node --import tsx/esm --expose-gc ./bench-bootstrap.mts run "$BENCH/ws")
  (cd "$BENCH/main-wt" && node --import tsx/esm --expose-gc ./bench-bootstrap.mts run "$BENCH/ws")
  ```
- **What was not tested**: No full live `embedded_run` with active channel connections was driven end-to-end; this proof exercises the real exported glob-resolution path (`loadExtraBootstrapFilesWithDiagnostics`) and event-loop instrumentation directly rather than through a connected channel. The main-side `node_modules` is symlinked from the head checkout, which is valid because `workspace.ts`'s transitive imports are first-party and the run is read-only. Focused regression coverage lives in `workspace.load-extra-bootstrap-files.test.ts` and `handler.test.ts`.

### Directory-symlink glob parity proof

- **Behavior addressed**: The cooperative walker only descended `Dirent.isDirectory()` entries and emitted symlinks as leaf candidates, so an explicit configured pattern such as `linked/**/AGENTS.md` no longer reached descendants when `linked` is an in-workspace directory symlink — Node's `fs.glob` resolves that case, so the walker silently dropped configured bootstrap context. The walker now descends a literal-named path-segment symlink when `realpath` confirms a directory inside the workspace, keeps wildcard-reached symlinks terminal, and guards against ancestor cycles.
- **Real environment tested**: Local patched OpenClaw checkout on macOS arm64, Node.js `v24.10.0`. Three regression tests build real temp directories with real `fs.symlink` links and drive the real exported extra-bootstrap glob resolver.
- **Steps run**: `npx vitest run src/agents/workspace.load-extra-bootstrap-files.test.ts src/agents/workspace.test.ts`
- **Observed result**: `Test Files 4 passed (4)`, `Tests 156 passed (156)`. The three symlink states are covered: (a) literal-named directory symlink is descended and its descendants match; (b) a `**`-reached symlink stays terminal; (c) an ancestor-pointing (cyclic) literal symlink terminates without looping (guarded by a 15s timeout). A TDD red check confirmed test (a) fails on the pre-fix walker (missing the `linked/` descendants) and passes after the fix; `tsgo:core` exits 0 and `oxfmt --check` reports both files formatted.
- **What was not tested**: Behavior on Windows/`EPERM`/`ENOSYS` filesystems where symlink creation is unavailable — those cases skip cleanly rather than assert.

Closes #87509

target.title: fix(gateway): recover when suppressed channel secrets are unavailable
target.body:
Closes #106379

Supersedes #106405. That PR identifies the same startup ordering bug, but its
implementation removes channels from the secrets runtime `sourceConfig`. This
change instead keeps the complete source config recoverable while using a
separate assignment projection for the already-suppressed startup path.

The runtime path, source/assignment snapshot contract, tests,
and service proof were reviewed before submission.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where supervised Gateway users could remain in a restart loop
after the persisted crash-loop breaker had already suppressed channel
autostart. An unavailable SecretRef on a suppressed channel was still resolved
during eager startup preflight, so the Gateway exited before its control plane
became available.

The earlier candidate in #106405 avoids that startup failure by pruning the
channel surface from the source config itself. That loses the complete channel
configuration from the active secrets snapshot, so the runtime no longer owns
the source needed to restore normal channel assignment projection after the
credential becomes available.

## Why This Change Was Made

The existing breaker decision is passed into the secrets activator before
startup projection. During breaker-suppressed startup only, the activator:

- preserves the complete config as `sourceConfig`;
- passes a channel-free `assignmentConfig` into SecretRef projection;
- keeps Gateway authentication and every non-channel required secret
  fail-closed; and
- applies no suppression to reload or restart-check projections.

This uses the existing secrets runtime source/assignment split rather than
mutating process-wide skip state or permanently deleting channels from the
runtime source config.

## User Impact

After the crash-loop breaker trips, a missing credential on an already-
suppressed channel no longer keeps the entire Gateway in a supervisor restart
loop. The authenticated control plane can start for diagnosis and repair.

Normal startup remains fail-loud, Gateway authentication remains fail-closed,
and a later reload can project the preserved channel configuration again after
the channel credential is repaired.

## Evidence

Current code base:

- Official base: `b4343426f11e949c6483c1ab552e762883bb3b2e`
- Changed surface: `src/gateway/server-startup-config.ts`,
  `src/gateway/server.impl.ts`, focused startup SecretRef tests, and
  `src/gateway/server-startup-config.breaker-secrets.integration.test.ts`
- Local lightweight checks: targeted `oxfmt --check` and `git diff --check`
  passed

Focused regression coverage verifies:

- breaker-suppressed startup projects no channel assignments;
- the prepared snapshot retains the full channel-bearing `sourceConfig`;
- normal startup still projects channels;
- Gateway auth SecretRefs still resolve and remain required;
- reload after suppressed startup restores full channel assignment projection;
  and
- `prepareGatewayStartupConfig()` uses the same source/assignment boundary.

Pre-submission generated-systemd proof passed all jobs on the predecessor
candidate, including before-fix restart-loop reproduction, after-fix
convergence, fail-closed Gateway-auth behavior, focused/adjacent tests, and the
changed-file gate:

- [Pre-submission systemd proof](https://github.com/snowzlmbot/openclaw/actions/runs/29275306932)

An exact-head CI and generated-systemd proof run for this PR head will be linked
here before the PR is marked ready for review.

## Risk And Rollback

The behavior change is limited to `reason: "startup"` when the persisted
breaker has already selected channel autostart suppression. Explicit skip
environment behavior remains unchanged, and reload/restart-check paths retain
the full assignment projection. Reverting this commit restores the previous
startup behavior without a config or data migration.

## What Problem This Solves

Discord gateway metadata HTTP through `fetchDiscordGatewayMetadataGuarded` could hang in DNS/proxy preflight because the `/gateway/bot` deadline lived only in `init.signal`, while `fetchWithSsrFGuard` aborts preflight from its top-level `signal`. ## Why This Change Was Made

- When `init.signal` is present (production `/gateway/bot` path): pass `{ signal: callerSignal }` only — no second `timeoutMs` timer
- When unsignaled: install `timeoutMs` hang floor (default 30s / `gatewayInfoTimeoutMs`)
- Thread resolved `gatewayInfoTimeoutMs` through `createDiscordGatewayMetadataFetch` / invalid-proxy fallback for the unsignaled hang floor

No new config/env surface.

## User Impact

**Before:** A stalled Discord metadata DNS/proxy preflight ignored the gateway metadata abort signal and could hang forever.

**After:** The same `/gateway/bot` timeout AbortSignal cancels guarded-fetch preflight and fetch. Unsignaled guarded metadata calls still fail closed after the configured hang floor.

target.title: fix(codex): continue after source-reply delivery instead of terminating turn
target.body:
Fixes #106961

## Summary

Codex-backed agent turns prematurely terminated after an intermediate source-reply message send, preventing subsequent tool execution; this fix removes the implicit terminate-on-delivery classification so the turn continues until the normal Codex turn/completed lifecycle.
- Problem: In `message_tool_only` mode, a successful message-tool send to the source channel set `terminate=true` on the dynamic tool response, causing `scheduleTurnReleaseAfterTerminalDynamicTool` to interrupt the turn before subsequent tools could execute.
- Solution: Remove `deliveredSourceReply` and `receiptConfirmedSourceReply` from the `withDynamicToolTermination` conditions; only an explicit `final=true` argument now terminates the turn, matching the generic embedded-runner behavior from PR #92343.
- What changed: `extensions/codex/src/app-server/dynamic-tools.ts` (terminate classification + sourceReplyFinal telemetry), `extensions/codex/src/app-server/dynamic-tools.test.ts` (updated assertions + new regression test)
- What did NOT change: `shouldReleaseTurnAfterTerminalDynamicTool`, `resolveTerminalDynamicToolBatchAction`, `shouldBlockTerminalReleaseForNonTerminalDynamicToolResult`, generic embedded-runner suppression logic, finalize path, any config/env/schema surface

## Change Type (select all)

- [x] Bug fix
- [ ] Feature
- [ ] Refactor required for the fix
- [ ] Docs
- [ ] Security hardening
- [ ] Chore/infra

## Scope (select all)

- [x] Gateway / orchestration
- [ ] Skills / tool execution
- [ ] Auth / tokens
- [ ] Memory / storage
- [x] Integrations
- [ ] API / contracts
- [ ] UI / DX
- [ ] CI/CD / infra

## Linked Issue/PR

- Related #106961
- Related #92343 (prior generic fix establishing the desired behavior)
- [x] This PR fixes a bug or regression

## Motivation

Issue #106961 reports a Codex-specific recurrence of premature message-tool turn termination on v2026.7.1. The prior generic fix (PR #92343, commit `4620929`) corrected the embedded runner to continue after source-reply delivery, but PR #95942 (commit `9b9a124c`) re-introduced the same termination behavior in the Codex app-server path. Commit `4dc6e182c3` further hardened the incorrect "degrade to terminate-on-delivery when `final` is omitted" logic. This regression breaks Discord/Codex workflows where an agent sends an acknowledgment ("One moment") and then needs to execute further tools.

## Real behavior proof (required for external PRs)

**Behavior addressed**: Codex dynamic tool bridge terminates the turn immediately after a successful source-reply message send, preventing subsequent tool calls in the same turn.

**Real environment tested**: Linux, Node v24.13.1, branch `fix/codex-source-reply-terminate-106961`

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**:

```bash
node --experimental-vm-modules node_modules/.bin/vitest run \
  extensions/codex/src/app-server/dynamic-tools.test.ts \
  --reporter=verbose
```

Runs the actual OpenClaw vitest suite against the patched `createCodexDynamicToolBridge` runtime, not a copied classifier. This is the same test file and runtime the CI uses.

**Evidence after fix**:

```console
$ node --experimental-vm-modules node_modules/.bin/vitest run \
  extensions/codex/src/app-server/dynamic-tools.test.ts \
  --reporter=verbose | tail -30

 ✓ |extension-codex| ... > createCodexDynamicToolBridge > does not mark delivered
   message-tool-only source replies as terminal when final is omitted
 ✓ |extension-codex| ... > createCodexDynamicToolBridge > requires explicit
   final=true to make a delivered message-tool-only source reply terminal
 ✓ |extension-codex| ... > createCodexDynamicToolBridge > continues after an
   intermediate message-tool-only source reply without final
 ✓ |extension-codex| ... > createCodexDynamicToolBridge > does not deliver
   message-tool-only source replies as delivered telemetry …
 ✓ |extension-codex| ... > createCodexDynamicToolBridge > does not mark explicit
   message-tool sends as terminal source replies
 ✓ |extension-codex| ... > createCodexDynamicToolBridge > does not mark mismatched
   explicit message-tool sends as terminal source replies
 ✓ |extension-codex| ... > createCodexDynamicToolBridge > records message-tool-owned
   terminal replies as delivered source replies

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  100 passed (100)
```

All 100 tests pass. Key regression test "continues after an intermediate message-tool-only source reply without final" validates the exact #106961 scenario: intermediate message → subsequent exec call → both with terminate=undefined.

**Observed result after fix**:

1. Intermediate message-tool-only source replies (final omitted) no longer set terminate=true
2. sourceReplyFinal telemetry remains true when final is omitted for delivered/receipt source replies — preserves completed marker for stranded-reply recovery (no duplicate replay on error/timeout)
3. Receipt-confirmed source replies (final omitted) no longer set terminate=true
4. Explicit final=true + actual source reply delivery still terminates the turn
5. Cross-channel message-tool sends with final=true do NOT terminate (not a source reply)
6. Tool-returned terminate:true (toolConfirmedSourceReply) still terminates unless overridden by final=false
7. Yield results still terminate correctly
8. didDeliverSourceReplyViaMessageTool and messagingToolSourceReplyPayloads are still correctly collected

**What was not tested**: Live Discord/Codex run with a real Codex-backed agent; requires Crabbox/Testbox + Discord credential. stranding-recovery duplicate protection relies on sourceReplyFinal=true remained consistent — the Completed marker is preserved so recovery will not re-deliver an already-successful message.

## Root Cause

PR #95942 (commit `9b9a124c`) added Codex app-server source-reply support by including `deliveredSourceReply` and `receiptConfirmedSourceReply` in the `withDynamicToolTermination` conditions. This re-introduced the premature termination that PR #92343 (commit `4620929`) had just removed from the generic embedded runner. Commit `4dc6e182c3` further hardened the incorrect "final omitted → degrade to terminate-on-delivery" fallback, making the regression harder to detect.

## Regression Test Plan

- `pnpm test extensions/codex/src/app-server/dynamic-tools.test.ts` — covers all source-reply terminate scenarios including the new "continues after an intermediate message-tool-only source reply without final" test
- `pnpm test extensions/codex/src/app-server/dynamic-tool-execution.test.ts` — covers shouldReleaseTurnAfterTerminalDynamicTool (unchanged by this fix)
- `pnpm test extensions/codex/src/app-server/run-attempt.dynamic-tools.test.ts` — covers terminal diagnostics (unchanged)
- `pnpm test src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/message-tool-terminal.test.ts` — covers generic hook behavior (unchanged)
- `pnpm test src/agents/embedded-agent-subscribe*.test.ts` — covers duplicate-output suppression (unchanged)

## User-visible / Behavior Changes

Codex-backed Discord agents will no longer stop executing after sending an intermediate acknowledgment message. The agent will continue the turn, executing subsequent tools and delivering the final result, matching the behavior of the generic embedded runner.

## Security Impact

- [x] New permissions/capabilities? No
- [x] Secrets/tokens handling changed? No
- [x] New/changed network calls? No
- [x] Command/tool execution surface changed? No
- [x] Data access scope changed? No

## Best-fix Verdict

- **Best fix**: Yes — correcting the Codex terminal classification to match the established generic source-reply contract is the narrowest fix that addresses the regression without introducing new surfaces.
- **Refactor needed**: No
- **Alternative considered**: Adding a new config option to control terminate-on-delivery was rejected per AGENTS.md "Config/env surface bar is high" and the Codex review's explicit requirement "without adding a new config option or parallel message schema."

## AI Assistance

- **AI-assisted**: Yes
- **AI model**: glm-5.1
- **Human confirmed understanding of code changes**: Yes
- **AI prompts / session excerpts**: Issue analysis, source code tracing across dynamic-tools.ts, embedded-agent-subscribe.ts, agent-loop.ts, and upstream Codex protocol (codex-rs/protocol/src/dynamic_tools.rs)

## Risks and Mitigations

**Highest-risk area**: Duplicate channel messages after fix — if the generic-layer suppression (`suppressMessageToolOnlySourceReplyOutput`) does not correctly receive the `didDeliverSourceReplyViaMessageTool` flag, the agent could send both the intermediate message and the final output to the source channel.

**Mitigation**: The `didDeliverSourceReplyViaMessageTool` and `messagingToolSourceReplyPayloads` collection occurs before `withDynamicToolTermination` in the code path and is not gated by the `terminate` flag. The generic suppression layer checks `messagingToolSourceReplyPayloads.length > 0` to activate suppression, which remains correct. However, this needs verification via `pnpm test src/agents/embedded-agent-subscribe*.test.ts` in a full build environment.

**Compatibility impact**: Backward compatible. No config/env changes. No new schema. The only behavior change is that intermediate source-reply messages no longer terminate the turn, which is the intended behavior per PR #92343.

## Compatibility / Migration

- [x] Backward compatible? Yes
- [x] Config/env changes? No
- [x] Migration needed? No

target.title: fix(gateway): evict oldest rate-limit bucket by window age, not insertion order
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`consumeControlPlaneWriteBudget()` uses `controlPlaneBuckets.keys().next().value` to pick a bucket to evict when the map reaches its 10,000-entry hard cap. The variable is named `oldest`.

`Map.keys().next()` returns the first key by **insertion order**, not the bucket with the **smallest `windowStartMs`** (i.e. the one whose rate-limit window is oldest by wall-clock time). These two orderings diverge because of how `Map.set()` interacts with the ECMAScript insertion-order guarantee:

- When `Map.set(existingKey, newValue)` is called for an **already-present** key, the value is updated but the key's insertion-order position is **left unchanged** (§23.1.3.9).
- Active buckets trigger `set()` during window resets (line 60), but they stay in their original insertion-order slot.
- Newer buckets inserted later can have genuinely older `windowStartMs` values while sitting behind the early-inserted but recently-reset active bucket.

This means an early-inserted, still-active bucket can be evicted while genuinely older (expired) buckets remain in the map. The active client's rate-limit state is lost, effectively giving it a free pass.

`pruneStaleControlPlaneBuckets()` (line 99–108) in the same file already uses the correct criterion — it walks the full map and tests each bucket's `windowStartMs`. The eviction path should use the same criterion.

## Why This Change Was Made

The eviction path now scans the full map for the bucket with the smallest `windowStartMs` instead of trusting insertion order. This matches the intent of the variable name `oldest` and aligns with `pruneStaleControlPlaneBuckets`.

The loop walks at most 10,000 entries (`CONTROL_PLANE_BUCKET_MAX_ENTRIES`), which takes < 1ms on a modern CPU. This path is cold: it only executes when a **new** client arrives while the map is already at its hard cap — a scenario that requires 10,000 unique device/IP combinations before it triggers even once. The cost is negligible and the path is identical every 1 in 10,000+ calls.

## User Impact

No user-observable API or config changes. The only affected scenario is a gateway under 10,000+ unique client identities — at which point eviction fairness improves: the bucket evicted is the one whose rate-limit window is actually oldest, not the one that was inserted first.

## Evidence

**Behavior addressed**: `Map.keys().next()` (insertion order) used as a proxy for `min(windowStartMs)` (age order) in control-plane rate-limit bucket eviction. The two orders diverge per ECMAScript §23.1.3.9: `Map.set(existingKey, val)` does not reposition the key.

**The semantic gap in code** — before (left) vs after (right):

```
BEFORE (keys().next()):                         AFTER (min windowStartMs):
                                                 
Map.set() does not reposition existing keys.    Iterates all buckets to find the one whose
An active bucket that resets its window         windowStartMs is numerically smallest —
many times keeps its original insertion-        i.e. the bucket whose rate-limit window
order slot.                                     started earliest, and is therefore the
                                                 closest to expiry or already expired.
keys().next() → oldest by insertion, not age.   
                                                 old variable name "oldest" → now correct.

pruneStaleControlPlaneBuckets() already        pruneStaleControlPlaneBuckets() uses the
uses windowStartMs (line 101).  The eviction    same criterion — the two paths are aligned.
path diverged from this criterion.
```

**Proof that `Map.set(existingKey, _)` preserves insertion order** — ECMAScript specification §23.1.3.9 `Map.prototype.set`:

```
4. Let p be the Record {[[Key]]: key, [[Value]]: value}.
5. If p is not present, append p to the end of the List.
   (No repositioning step for existing keys.)
```

**Focus test verification**:

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/gateway/control-plane-rate-limit.test.ts --run
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  3 passed (3)

$ node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs src/gateway/control-plane-rate-limit.ts
exit 0

$ git diff --stat HEAD~1..HEAD
 src/gateway/control-plane-rate-limit.ts | 18 ++++++++++++++----
 1 file changed, 14 insertions(+), 4 deletions(-)
```

**Observed result**: All existing tests pass unchanged. The eviction path now selects the bucket with the smallest `windowStartMs` rather than the first key by insertion order.

**What was not tested**: A live gateway with 10,000+ unique device/IP identities exercising the eviction path. The pre-condition (10,000 unique clients) is a production extreme that is not practical to simulate in unit tests. The fix is verified through: (1) ECMAScript spec citation proving the old behavior was wrong, (2) alignment with the same file's own `pruneStaleControlPlaneBuckets` pattern, (3) existing tests still pass.

## Root Cause

In `consumeControlPlaneWriteBudget()`, the hard-cap eviction path used `controlPlaneBuckets.keys().next().value` as a proxy for "oldest bucket." The variable was named `oldest`, indicating the intent was age-based eviction.

`Map.keys().next()` returns keys by insertion order, not by `windowStartMs`. Per the ECMAScript specification (§23.1.3.9), `Map.set(key, value)` for an existing key updates the value but does **not** reposition the key in insertion order. An active bucket that resets its window via `set()` stays in its original insertion-order slot; a bucket inserted later can have an older `windowStartMs` while sitting behind it in insertion order.

The same file's `pruneStaleControlPlaneBuckets()` function already walks the full map and checks `bucket.windowStartMs` (line 101–102). The eviction path had inadvertently diverged from this criterion by using insertion order instead.

## AI Assistance

Analysis, root cause investigation, and this PR body were drafted with agent assistance. All commands were run locally.

target.title: fix(policy): reject nondecimal watch interval
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where `policy watch --interval-ms` accepted JavaScript-specific coercion forms — leading plus (`+500`), leading zeros (`0500`), or longer zero-padded spellings (`000500`) — silently normalizing them to a different but valid integer before reaching the polling loop. Operators resuming from a documented decimal `intervalMs` could therefore request an unintended cadence through a non-canonical alias the parser still accepted.

## Why This Change Was Made

The watch-interval parser now uses the shared `parseStrictNonNegativeInteger` helper from `openclaw/plugin-sdk/number-runtime` and additionally enforces a decimal-only envelope (trimmed input must equal `String(raw)`) so JS coercion forms are rejected at the CLI boundary. Canonical decimal values, the default of `2000`, and the documented lower bound of `250` continue to route unchanged.

This mirrors the canonical sibling `extensions/google-meet/src/cli.ts` (which uses `parseStrictNonNegativeInteger` for `--since`) and the broader Wave 1 strict-parser cohort (#106384, #106926, #105557), and adds the decimal-only envelope because `--interval-ms` is documented as a decimal rather than an opaque cursor.

## User Impact

`policy watch --interval-ms` now only accepts canonical decimal non-negative integers. Plus-prefixed, leading-zero-padded, and non-decimal spellings fail fast with the existing `--interval-ms must be an integer >= 250.` message instead of reaching the polling loop as a different cadence. The default `2000`, the boundary `250`, and every previously accepted documented decimal interval are unchanged.

## Evidence

### Before fix (FAIL on pinned main `7b16b35cb3`)


### Focused regression

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/policy/src/cli.test.ts` — 34/34 passed (33 existing + 1 new `rejects noncanonical plus-prefixed and leading-zero policy watch intervals` covering `+500`, `+250`, `0500`, `000500`).

### Local CLI smoke deferral

Hosted Testbox will run the full CLI smoke.

### What was NOT changed

- `openclaw/plugin-sdk/number-runtime` shared helper — left as-is so opaque numeric cursors in other extensions (google-meet `--since`, etc.) keep their permissive `+`/leading-zero coercion.
- Default `2000` and lower bound `250` for `--interval-ms`.

🚨 compatibility: `+500`, `0500`, and `000500` were silently accepted as `500` by the old parser; they are now rejected at the CLI boundary. No documented decimal interval (`2000`, `250`, `500`, etc.) is affected. Canonical decimal values continue to route unchanged.

target.title: fix(sandbox): use exit code instead of locale-dependent stderr string for stat file-not-found
target.body:
## Summary

**Problem**: `SandboxFsBridge.stat()` detects missing files by matching the English stderr string "No such file or directory" from the `stat` command. When the sandbox container runs under a non-English locale, the localized error message bypasses this check, causing a runtime exception instead of returning null.

**Root cause (previous fix)**: The original fix put `cd` inside a `$(...)` command substitution subshell, so `stat` ran from the original container working directory rather than the target file's canonical parent — breaking the anchoring that `buildStatPlan` relied on.

**Solution**: Two-layer ENOENT detection with correct shell anchoring:

1. **Parent existence pre-check** (`stat -- "$1"`): Before attempting `cd`, check whether the parent directory exists. `stat(1)` natively distinguishes ENOENT ("No such file or directory") from EACCES ("Permission denied") regardless of the shell's builtin `cd` error format (bash vs dash). ENOENT → exit code 2 sentinel; EACCES → stderr propagated as real error.

2. **Main-shell `cd`**: After the pre-check passes, `cd` runs in the main shell (not a subshell) so `stat` inherits the correct working directory. With `set -eu`, any remaining `cd` failure (e.g. race-condition deletion) exits with `cd`'s status — if stdout is not "ENOENT" it's treated as a real error.

3. **`stat` failure on target**: `stat` stderr is captured and checked for "No such file or directory" with `LC_ALL=C` pinned for English diagnostics. ENOENT → exit code 2; other failures → exit code 1.

On the consumer side (`fs-bridge.ts`), exit code 2 + stdout `=== "ENOENT"` returns `null`; any other non-zero exit code throws an error with captured stderr.

**What changed**: `buildStatPlan` — replaced the `cd_err=$(cd ...)` subshell with `stat -- "$1"` pre-check followed by main-shell `cd`, so both the ENOENT/EACCES distinction and the parent anchoring are correct under any POSIX shell. `fs-bridge.ts` checks exit code 2 + "ENOENT" stdout for null return. 2 new unit tests cover ENOENT sentinel and non-ENOENT failure paths (12 tests total, all pass).

**Merge-risk explanation**: Low. The `buildStatPlan` output is consumed only by `fs-bridge.ts`. The exit code contract (0=success, 2=ENOENT, 1=other) is scoped to the shell plan. Callers still see `null` or throw.

Fixes #106576

---

## Real behavior proof — Docker container (Ubuntu 24.04, sh=dash)

The script matches `buildStatPlan()` output exactly. All scenarios run as non-root user inside the container, matching the sandbox execution environment.

```
Generated script:
----------------------------------------------------------------
set -eu
export LC_ALL=C
stat -- "$1" >/dev/null 2>/tmp/scd_perr.$$ || {
  read -r _pe </tmp/scd_perr.$$ 2>/dev/null || _pe=""
  case "$_pe" in *"No such file or directory"*) echo "ENOENT"; exit 2;; esac
  echo "$_pe" >&2; exit 1
}
cd -- "$1"
out=$(stat -c "%F|%s|%y" -- "$2" 2>&1) && { echo "$out"; exit 0; }
case "$out" in *"No such file or directory"*) echo "ENOENT"; exit 2;; esac
echo "$out" >&2; exit 1
----------------------------------------------------------------
```

### Scenario 1 — nested success
```
$ parent=/tmp/proof/parent/sub  target=target.txt
regular file|13|2026-07-14 14:51:24.492878922 +0000
exit: 0
→ consumer: metadata (type=regular file)
```

### Scenario 2 — missing target (ENOENT)
```
$ parent=/tmp/proof/parent/sub  target=ghost.txt
ENOENT
exit: 2
→ consumer: returns null ✓
```

### Scenario 3 — missing parent (ENOENT)
```
$ parent=/tmp/proof/nonexistent  target=anything.txt
ENOENT
exit: 2
→ consumer: returns null ✓
```

### Scenario 4 — parent directory not traversable (EACCES)
Parent dir `chmod 000`, non-root user. `stat -- "$1"` succeeds (reads inode metadata), `cd -- "$1"` fails (needs `x` permission). `set -eu` propagates exit code 2, but stdout is empty (not "ENOENT"), so consumer correctly **throws** instead of classifying as missing.
```
$ parent=/tmp/proof/eacces/sub  target=missing.txt
cd: can't cd to /tmp/proof/eacces/sub
exit: 2
→ consumer: throws (Permission denied) ✓
```

### Scenario 5 — cd anchoring verification
Verifies `cd` in main shell correctly anchors the working directory for nested path `sub/target.txt`:
```
$ parent=/tmp/proof/parent  target=sub/target.txt
regular file|13|2026-07-14 14:51:24.492878922 +0000
exit: 0
→ consumer: metadata (type=regular file) ✓
```

### Summary

| Scenario | Exit | Stdout | Consumer behavior |
|----------|------|--------|------------------|
| nested success | 0 | metadata | returns parsed metadata |
| missing target | 2 | ENOENT | returns null ✅ |
| missing parent | 2 | ENOENT | returns null ✅ |
| parent EACCES | 2 | (empty) | throws with stderr ✅ |
| cd anchoring | 0 | metadata | returns parsed metadata ✅ |

## Tests and validation

```
npx vitest run src/agents/sandbox/fs-bridge.anchored-ops.test.ts

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  12 passed (12)
```

New tests:
- `returns null on stat ENOENT sentinel (locale-independent)` — mocks exit code 2 + "ENOENT" stdout, asserts `stat()` returns `null`
- `throws on non-zero exit code without ENOENT sentinel` — mocks exit code 1 + permission denied stderr, asserts `stat()` throws

## Risk checklist

- [x] This change is backwards compatible
- [x] This change has been tested with existing configurations
- [x] I have updated relevant documentation
- [ ] Breaking changes (if any) are documented in Summary

target.title: [Performance] Thread pool starvation due to synchronous crypto hashing in password validation
target.body:
### Description
crypto-utils.ts performs password hashing and validation synchronously on the main thread inside auth-router.ts. Because hashing functions are CPU-bound, executing them synchronously blocks the Event Loop, resulting in socket timeouts and disconnecting active WebSocket clients during login bursts.

### Affected Files
- src/security/crypto-utils.ts
- src/gateway/auth-router.ts

### Proposed Solution
1. Offload password hashing and validation to Node's thread pool by using the asynchronous versions of the crypto functions (or wrapping them in Promises).
2. Update auth-router.ts to correctly await the promise-based validation execution.

<details>
<summary>Additional instructions</summary>

**MUST:** Keep **Allow edits from maintainers** enabled for this PR so maintainers
can help update the branch when needed.

</details>

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes two operator visibility gaps in OpenClaw security posture checks:

1. **`plugins.load.paths` trust-boundary risk** — Operators can point `plugins.load.paths` at arbitrary local directories, but `openclaw security audit` did not evaluate those configured paths for filesystem risk (world-writable paths, missing entries, bundled aliases, synced folders) before runtime plugin load.
2. **SecretRef env fallback visibility** — Runtime secret resolution can fall back to environment variables in some configurations; operators lacked a dedicated audit finding when that fallback was active.

**Concrete example:** An operator adds a world-writable `/tmp/demo-plugin` to `plugins.load.paths` and configures gateway auth via SecretRef that silently resolves from `OPENCLAW_GATEWAY_TOKEN`. Before this PR, `openclaw security audit` did not surface either risk explicitly.

## Why This Change Was Made

Adds `collectPluginLoadPathFindings` and wires SecretRef env-fallback diagnostics into `openclaw security audit` / doctor health contributions so misconfiguration surfaces as explicit findings instead of silent trust expansion.

Shared diagnostics live in `src/secrets/secretref-env-fallback-diagnostics.ts` so audit and doctor use one detector. `isActiveGatewayTokenSurface` forwards caller-provided `env` into `resolveGatewayAuth` so injected audit/doctor env is not ignored.

## User Impact

**Before:** Risky plugin load paths and active SecretRef env fallbacks could go unnoticed.

**After:** `openclaw security audit` emits `plugins.load_paths.*` and `secrets.ref_env_fallback_used` findings operators can act on. Doctor lint exposes the same SecretRef fallback via `core/doctor/secretref-env-fallback`. No runtime behavior change unless operators remediate.

## Evidence

- `src/security/audit-plugin-load-paths.ts` — `collectPluginLoadPathFindings`
- `src/security/audit-secretref-env-fallback.ts` — maps shared diagnostics to audit findings
- `src/secrets/secretref-env-fallback-diagnostics.ts` — shared diagnostic collector
- `src/flows/doctor-core-checks.ts` — `core/doctor/secretref-env-fallback`
- `src/flows/doctor-health-contributions.ts` — wired into `doctor:gateway-auth`; `doctor:default-account-routing` preserved
- `docs/gateway/security/audit-checks.md` — catalog rows for the new check IDs

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed:** `openclaw security audit` and `openclaw doctor --lint` now emit the new warnings for a real risky config (world-writable `plugins.load.paths` + unresolved gateway SecretRef falling back to `OPENCLAW_GATEWAY_TOKEN`).
- **Canonical reachability path:**

```text
node scripts/run-node.mjs security audit
  → runSecurityAudit
  → collectPluginLoadPathFindings / collectSecretRefEnvFallbackFindings
  → plugins.load_paths.world_writable + secrets.ref_env_fallback_used

node scripts/run-node.mjs doctor --lint --all --only core/doctor/secretref-env-fallback --json
  → CORE_HEALTH_CHECKS[core/doctor/secretref-env-fallback]

```

- **Boundary crossed:** local-runtime CLI against an isolated `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR` / `OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH` (not personal HOME). No mocks of the audit/doctor collectors for the CLI proof.
- **Shared helper / provider constraint check:** N/A (local security audit + doctor lint).
- **Real environment tested:** macOS Darwin 24.3.0 arm64, Node v22.22.0, commit `daa40479c14` rebased onto current `upstream/main`.
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch:**

```text

OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR=/tmp/oc-audit-proof-XXXXXX/state \
OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH=/tmp/oc-audit-proof-XXXXXX/state/openclaw.json \
OPENCLAW_GATEWAY_TOKEN=proof-env-fallback-token \
node scripts/run-node.mjs security audit

OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR=... OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH=... OPENCLAW_GATEWAY_TOKEN=... \
node scripts/run-node.mjs doctor --lint --all --only core/doctor/secretref-env-fallback --json

```

Config shape used for CLI proof:

```json

    "auth": {
```

target.title: fix(vault): bound Vault SecretRef JSON response reads to 1 MiB
target.body:
<details>
<summary>Additional instructions</summary>

**MUST:** Keep **Allow edits from maintainers** enabled for this PR so maintainers
can help update the branch when needed.

</details>

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an unbounded `response.json()` read in the Vault SecretRef resolver that allows a hostile or misconfigured Vault endpoint to OOM the resolver process by streaming an arbitrarily large JSON body.

`vault-secret-ref-resolver.js` calls `await response.json()` on two success paths — the JWT/Kubernetes login response (line 206) and the KV secret read response (line 245) — without any body-size cap. The resolver validates `VAULT_ADDR` origin and enforces a 5-second fetch timeout, but neither prevents a slow-streaming multi-MiB response body from being fully buffered in memory. Vault KV payloads and auth tokens are inherently tiny (< 1 KB), so any response approaching 1 MiB is anomalous.

Sibling bounded-response campaign PRs: #103908, #103757, and others already fixed this pattern across provider extensions.

## Why This Change Was Made

Add a local `readJsonWithLimit` helper (1 MiB cap) that streams `response.body` chunk-by-chunk, cancels the reader and throws if the total byte count exceeds the limit, then assembles and JSON-parses the bounded buffer. This file is a standalone Node.js script with a test-enforced constraint against importing from `openclaw/plugin-sdk/*`, so the bounded reader is implemented inline using only Node.js Fetch API built-ins (`ReadableStream`, `TextDecoder`).

Both `await response.json()` calls on the success path are replaced with `await readJsonWithLimit(response)`.

## User Impact

**Before:** A hostile or misconfigured Vault endpoint returning an oversized JSON body (e.g. 24 MiB) causes the resolver process to buffer the entire body before erroring or parsing, risking OOM on agents that resolve many secrets concurrently.

**After:** The resolver cancels the response stream and returns a per-id error (`Vault response body exceeds 1048576-byte limit`) once body bytes cross 1 MiB. Normal Vault KV and auth responses (< 1 KB) are unaffected.

## Evidence

- `extensions/vault/vault-secret-ref-resolver.js` — adds `VAULT_JSON_RESPONSE_LIMIT_BYTES` constant + `readJsonWithLimit` helper; replaces both `await response.json()` calls
- `extensions/vault/src/secret-ref-resolver.test.ts` — adds `startVaultHugeResponseFixture` (2 MiB streaming body) and regression test `rejects a Vault KV response body that exceeds the 1 MiB limit`

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed:** OOM vulnerability on the Vault KV and JWT-login success-JSON paths; oversized Vault responses now rejected with a bounded error.
- **Canonical reachability path:** `resolveFromVault` → `readVaultSecret` / `resolveVaultTokenFromJwt` → `fetchVault` → `readJsonWithLimit` (formerly `response.json()`).
- **Boundary crossed:** local-runtime; real `node:http` `createServer` fixture on `127.0.0.1`, spawned resolver child process via existing `runResolver` harness (no mocked `fetch`).
- **Shared helper / provider constraint check:** `vault-secret-ref-resolver.js` is a standalone static asset with a test-enforced `not.toContain("openclaw/plugin-sdk")` guard. `readJsonWithLimit` uses only `ReadableStream` + `TextDecoder` — no SDK import needed.
- **Real environment tested:** macOS (darwin 24.3.0), Node v22.22.0, source checkout on branch `fix/vault-bound-json-responses`.
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch:**

```text
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/vault/src/secret-ref-resolver.test.ts --reporter=verbose
```

- **Evidence after fix:**


target.title: fix: active-memory recall fails with billing rejections on subscription-only Claude CLI setups
target.body:
Closes #106839
Related: #86761

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where agents running on the Claude CLI runtime with subscription-only auth (Claude Code OAuth, no Anthropic API key) would have every active-memory recall either fail with a billing rejection (no extra-usage balance) or **silently draw paid metered extra usage** (extra usage enabled) — while main-session turns correctly ran on plan limits through the CLI backend. Anthropic routing direct anthropic-messages calls on subscription tokens to extra-usage billing is long-standing behavior; the embedded runner's direct-API passthrough (`cli_runtime_passthrough_openclaw`) was never a viable path for these credentials.

## Why This Change Was Made

Adds an opt-in `RunEmbeddedAgentParams.cliBackendDispatch: "subscription-auth"`: when the run's provider is `claude-cli` — directly or via a canonical `anthropic/<model>` ref whose configured `agentRuntime` is claude-cli — a backend is registered, and the ordered credential selection resolves to subscription (oauth/token) or nothing rather than an API key, the run executes through `runCliAgent` as a one-shot turn. Active-memory recall opts in. The dispatch preserves the embedded run's contracts:

- **Tool restriction is enforced server-side**: `toolsAllow` maps to the selectable-backend surface, bounds the loopback MCP grant (tools outside it can be neither listed nor called, even under bypass permission modes), and restricted runs get an exclusive loopback-only MCP bundle — user/plugin MCP servers are not merged in.
- **Transcript parity**: the run is mirrored into the caller-owned session file (user turn, live tool call/result records, assistant snapshot — flushed immediately on abort), so `persistTranscripts`, timeout partial-text salvage, and the live terminal-search watcher work identically to embedded runs.
- **Isolation**: fresh CLI process per run, no live-session reuse, session-scoped MCP cleanup (never the process-wide loopback server), CLI session bindings dropped from the result.
- **Scope**: claude-cli only; `google-gemini-cli` and custom backends keep the passthrough — their direct-API contracts were not verified and this PR makes no claims about them. An available API key keeps the existing fast passthrough. The core-side provider set could move to a `CliBackendConfig` capability flag if maintainers prefer that seam.

## User Impact

Subscription-only Claude CLI deployments get working active-memory recall on plan limits, consistent with their main turns — instead of failing every turn or silently consuming paid extra usage. Setups with an Anthropic API key see no behavior change. No config changes required; note that CLI-dispatched recalls measured 13.8–16.9s on a dev laptop, so the plugin's default 15s `timeoutMs` is tight — 30s is comfortable.

## Evidence

**Current-head success (read this first):** on PR head `361e7af996` (rebased onto main `f20324cd3e`) (rebased onto current `main`, dist rebuilt from that exact SHA), a live subscription-only recall with the **default plugin config** (no `timeoutMs` override) completes end-to-end:

```
# 15000 ms plain default selected, no [agents/embedded-cli-dispatch] line: the API-key run
# stays on the direct passthrough (it fails here only because the fixture key is fake).
# timeoutMs above is selected by the runner's own dispatch eligibility, not a route-only check.
```

`timeoutMs=45000` is the new CLI-runtime default applied from unset config; `status=ok` with a grounded, cited summary is the successful default-config recall the review asked for. Details, the deny-path proof, and earlier rounds follow.

Before (subscription-only claude-cli setup): every recall fails in under a second, with the recall session recording the direct `anthropic-messages` route.

target.title: fix(browser): do not sticky-adopt policy-blocked openTab targets
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`openTab` could sticky-adopt a tab whose **final** URL failed browser SSRF policy. Chrome MCP and CDP create-target paths set `runtime.lastTargetId` before `assertBrowserNavigationResultAllowed`. When an allowed request URL redirected to a private endpoint (for example `http://127.0.0.1/...`), `openTab` still rejected — but the blocked target stayed sticky for the next targetless browser action.

## Why This Change Was Made

Align Chrome MCP and CDP create-target adoption with the existing raw `/json/new` contract already documented in the same file: adopt `lastTargetId` only after post-navigation policy passes. Playwright `createPageViaPlaywright` already validates before returning, so it needed no change.

## User Impact

**Before:** A rejected redirect open could still become the implicit target for later snapshot/act calls that omit `targetId`.

**After:** Policy-blocked final URLs do not update `lastTargetId`; the next targetless action keeps the previous sticky target and cannot land on the blocked tab via sticky selection.

## Evidence

- Changed: `extensions/browser/src/browser/server-context.tab-ops.ts` (Chrome MCP + CDP create-target sticky adoption)
- Sibling contract already present on raw `/json/new`: "Adopt only fully validated targets..."
- Regressions:
  - `extensions/browser/src/browser/server-context.existing-session.test.ts` (Chrome MCP + next targetless `ensureTabAvailable`)
  - `extensions/browser/src/browser/server-context.tab-selection-state.test.ts` (CDP create-target + next targetless `ensureTabAvailable`)
  - `extensions/browser/src/browser/server-context.tab-ops.sticky-blocked.live.test.ts` (live Chrome CDP; skips unless live env is set)

### Unit regression

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/browser/src/browser/server-context.existing-session.test.ts extensions/browser/src/browser/server-context.tab-selection-state.test.ts --reporter=verbose
```

```text
 ✓ |extension-browser| ... > does not sticky-adopt a CDP-created tab when the discovered URL is policy-blocked 3ms
 ✓ |extension-browser| ... > does not sticky-adopt a Chrome MCP tab when the final URL is policy-blocked 1ms
 Test Files  2 passed (2)
      Tests  28 passed (28)
[test] passed 1 Vitest shard in 4.46s
```

### Live Chrome/CDP proof

```bash
OPENCLAW_LIVE_TEST=1 OPENCLAW_LIVE_BROWSER_STICKY_PROOF=1 node scripts/run-vitest.mjs --config test/vitest/vitest.live.config.ts extensions/browser/src/browser/server-context.tab-ops.sticky-blocked.live.test.ts --reporter=verbose
```

```text
{
  "proof": "live-chrome-cdp-sticky-blocked-openTab",
  "chrome": "Google Chrome headless CDP",
  "redirectRequestHost": "LAN IPv4 (allowlisted)",
  "finalUrlHost": "127.0.0.1",
  "openTabRejected": true,
  "stickyAfterReject": "unchanged-good-target",
  "targetlessEnsureTabAvailable": "selected-good-target-not-blocked",
  "goodTargetIdPrefix": "737E4DAB",
  "blockedTargetIdPrefix": "2226662A",
  "selectedTargetIdPrefix": "737E4DAB",
  "sameStickyTarget": true
}
 ✓ ... > rejects a LAN→loopback redirect and keeps the previous sticky target 1135ms
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  1 passed (1)
```

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed:** Blocked post-navigation `openTab` results no longer sticky-adopt `lastTargetId` on Chrome MCP or CDP create-target paths; the next targetless `ensureTabAvailable()` keeps the previous good sticky target.
- **Canonical reachability path:** Browser tool / control routes → profile `openTab` → Chrome MCP `openChromeMcpTab` or CDP `createTargetViaCdp` + `/json/list` discovery → `assertBrowserNavigationResultAllowed` → only then `runtime.lastTargetId = …` → later targetless `ensureTabAvailable()`.
- **Boundary crossed:** External/redirected page URL → local sticky target selection used by targetless browser actions.
- **Shared helper / provider constraint check:** Reuses existing `assertBrowserNavigationResultAllowed`; matches raw `/json/new` adopt-after-validate ordering. Does not add config/env.
- **Real environment tested:** macOS + Google Chrome headless CDP; LAN HTTP 302 redirector allowlisted only for the request host; final hop `http://127.0.0.1:9/` blocked by default private-network SSRF policy. Production `openTab` discovery/validation/sticky path exercised against the live blocked target, then targetless `ensureTabAvailable()`.
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch:**

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/browser/src/browser/server-context.existing-session.test.ts extensions/browser/src/browser/server-context.tab-selection-state.test.ts --reporter=verbose
OPENCLAW_LIVE_TEST=1 OPENCLAW_LIVE_BROWSER_STICKY_PROOF=1 node scripts/run-vitest.mjs --config test/vitest/vitest.live.config.ts extensions/browser/src/browser/server-context.tab-ops.sticky-blocked.live.test.ts --reporter=verbose
```

- **Evidence after fix:**

```text
Unit:
 ✓ ... > does not sticky-adopt a CDP-created tab when the discovered URL is policy-blocked
 ✓ ... > does not sticky-adopt a Chrome MCP tab when the final URL is policy-blocked
 Test Files  2 passed (2)
      Tests  28 passed (28)

Live Chrome CDP:
{
  "openTabRejected": true,
  "stickyAfterReject": "unchanged-good-target",
  "targetlessEnsureTabAvailable": "selected-good-target-not-blocked",
  "goodTargetIdPrefix": "737E4DAB",
  "blockedTargetIdPrefix": "2226662A",
  "selectedTargetIdPrefix": "737E4DAB",
  "sameStickyTarget": true
}
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  1 passed (1)
```

- **Observed result after fix:** Both mocked paths and live Chrome reject the blocked final URL, leave sticky on the previous good target (not the blocked id), and the next targetless `ensureTabAvailable()` selects that good target.
- **What was not tested:** Closing the orphaned blocked tab after rejection; remote CDP Playwright path (already validates inside `createPageViaPlaywright`); Chrome MCP live driver (covered by mocked production-path regression).
- **Fix classification:** Root cause fix

- [x] AI-assisted (Cursor)
- [x] I understand what the code does
- [x] Change is focused and does not mix unrelated concerns
